items.prompt: In critical thinking, what is an assumption in an argument?

options.label: The final claim that the argument tries to establish
A piece of evidence offered by an outside expert
A belief the argument relies on but never states openly
A fact that has been proven by repeated experiments

rubric: An assumption is an unstated belief needed for the reasoning to work.
Distractors confuse it with proven facts, conclusions or expert evidence.

items.prompt: Which term names the fallacy of attacking the person making a claim instead of the claim itself?

options.label: Begging the question
Straw man
Red herring
Ad hominem

rubric: Ad hominem targets the person rather than the argument.
Straw man misrepresents the argument; the others are different fallacies.

items.prompt: What is the conclusion of an argument?

options.label: The background facts that the audience already knows
The strongest example that the speaker can offer
The claim that the premises are meant to support
The first statement that the speaker happens to make

rubric: The conclusion is the claim the premises aim to support.
Distractors confuse it with background, opening position or examples.

items.prompt: What is a straw man fallacy?

options.label: Relying on a famous person's opinion as proof
Predicting a chain of extreme events without support
Repeating the claim in different words as proof
Misrepresenting someone's position to make it easier to attack

rubric: A straw man distorts the opponent's position and then attacks the distortion.
Other options describe appeal to authority, circular reasoning and slippery slope.

items.prompt: What is a false dilemma (false dichotomy)?

options.label: Presenting only two options when more really exist
Choosing between two equally well-supported claims
Giving two reasons that contradict each other
Admitting that a question has no clear answer

rubric: A false dilemma wrongly limits the choices to two.
Distractors describe contradiction, uncertainty or a genuine choice.

items.prompt: Which of the following are named logical fallacies? Select all that apply.

options.label: Controlled experiment
Slippery slope
Bandwagon appeal
Ad hominem
Random sampling

rubric: Bandwagon, slippery slope and ad hominem are all fallacies.
Controlled experiments and random sampling are methods of gathering good evidence.

items.prompt: A shopper tells a friend, "Everyone at school is buying this phone, so it must be the best one." The friend wants to name the reasoning error in this statement. Which fallacy is it?

options.label: Circular reasoning
False dilemma
Bandwagon appeal
Straw man

rubric: Claiming something is best because many people choose it is a bandwagon appeal.
Other options name different fallacies that do not match the popularity claim.

items.prompt: Why is circular reasoning considered a flawed way to argue?

options.label: It offers too many reasons, so the main point becomes unclear
It uses emotional words, so the audience cannot judge fairly
Its premises are always false, so the conclusion must be false
Its conclusion is already assumed in its premises, so nothing new is shown

rubric: Circular reasoning assumes what it claims to prove, so it gives no real support.
Distractors confuse it with false premises, emotional appeals or overloading.

items.prompt: A school claims its tutoring program raises grades. Which evidence would best support the claim?

options.label: The fact that many families enrolled their children
A comparison of similar students with and without tutoring
A few students praising the program in interviews
A statement from the program's own director

rubric: A comparison group shows what happens without tutoring, so it supports the claim best.
Testimonials, popularity and the director's word do not isolate the program's effect.

items.prompt: A manager says, "If we allow one short break, soon nobody will work at all." How is this reasoning best classified?

options.label: Hasty generalisation
Appeal to authority
Ad hominem
Slippery slope

rubric: It predicts an extreme chain of events from one small step without support, which is a slippery slope.
Other fallacies involve authority, small samples or attacking a person.

items.prompt: An argument has a valid structure, but one of its premises is false. What can be said about it?

options.label: It is unsound, because a sound argument needs true premises
It is a fallacy, because every false premise is a fallacy
It is sound, because valid structure guarantees truth
It is persuasive, because validity alone proves the conclusion

rubric: Soundness requires both valid structure and true premises.
Distractors treat validity as enough to guarantee a true conclusion.

items.prompt: Ice cream sales and drowning incidents both rise in summer. What is the best interpretation?

options.label: Ice cream causes people to drown more often
Drownings make people buy more ice cream
The two are unrelated and the pattern is pure chance
Both are likely influenced by a third factor, hot weather

rubric: A shared cause, hot weather, explains why the two rise together without either causing the other.
Distractors assume direct causation or dismiss the pattern entirely.

items.prompt: Why is a single personal anecdote weak evidence for a general claim? Select all that apply.

options.label: It is too short to say anything useful at all
It cannot be an honest account of events
It rarely controls for other possible explanations
It may not be typical of other cases

rubric: An anecdote may be unrepresentative and does not rule out other explanations.
Honesty and length are not the reasons it is weak as general evidence.

items.prompt: A shop owner says, "Sales rose after we changed our logo, so the new logo caused the increase." A colleague wants to test whether this claim is well supported. Which question would be most useful?

options.label: Did sales rise in earlier months before the change?
Did the owner personally like the new logo design?
Did anything else change, such as prices, season or advertising?
Did competing shops also change their logos recently?

rubric: Checking for other changes tests whether the logo, rather than another factor, explains the rise.
Other questions are about taste or are less direct for ruling out alternative causes.

items.prompt: "Everyone at school is buying this phone, so it must be the best one." Which description fits this reasoning?

options.label: Bandwagon: popularity is treated as proof of quality
Ad hominem: the phone's makers are being attacked
False dilemma: only two choices are being offered
Straw man: an opponent's view is being distorted

rubric: The claim treats widespread buying as proof of quality, which is the bandwagon appeal.
Distractors name other fallacies; none involve attacking a person, distorting a view, or limiting choices.

items.prompt: Read: "Because the road is icy, you should drive slowly." Which statement is the conclusion?

options.label: You should drive slowly
The road is icy
Many drivers go too fast
Icy roads are dangerous

rubric: The conclusion is what the argument tries to establish; "because" marks the premise.
Learners who pick the icy road confuse the reason with the claim it supports.

items.prompt: Ice cream sales and drownings both rise in summer. What is the best interpretation of this pattern?

options.label: Ice cream causes cramps, so higher sales lead to drownings
Both rising together is pure chance, so the data mean nothing
Drownings upset people, so deaths push ice cream sales up
Hot weather likely raises both, so neither causes the other

rubric: A third factor (hot weather) plausibly drives both, so correlation does not show causation.
Distractors assert a causal link in either direction or dismiss the pattern as chance.

items.prompt: "She graduated from a top university, so she'll be a great manager." Which unstated assumption does this argument rely on?

options.label: Managers must always have attended a university
Graduates of top universities never fail at work
Her university is better than every other university
Academic prestige reliably predicts management ability

rubric: The argument needs a link between prestige and management skill, which is never stated.
Distractors are absolute or irrelevant claims that the argument does not need.

items.prompt: A school wants evidence that spaced practice helps students remember more. Which evidence would be strongest?

options.label: One top student who credits it for her good grades
A popular video in which many viewers praise the method
Two similar classes assigned at random, then given the same test
A teacher's strong impression after using it for one term

rubric: A comparison of similar, randomly assigned groups on the same test controls for other influences.
Testimonials, popularity and single cases are anecdotal and easily biased.

items.prompt: Which statements are examples of ad hominem reasoning (attacking the person instead of the argument)? Select all that apply.

options.label: His budget plan fails because it double-counts grant income.
Of course she backs the plan; she is too young to understand money.
The plan is flawed because it ignores rising rent costs.
Ignore his budget plan; he has been divorced twice.

rubric: Ad hominem dismisses a claim by targeting the speaker's personal traits rather than the reasoning.
The other two statements criticise the plan's content, which is legitimate.

items.prompt: A colleague notices that the last two emails with blue buttons got more clicks than usual. She concludes that blue buttons always boost clicks and wants every email changed. You are asked what is wrong with her reasoning.

options.label: She is attacking the people who wrote the earlier emails
Clicks are never a valid way to measure interest in an email
Her conclusion simply repeats its premise in different words
Two cases are too few to support a claim about "always"

rubric: Generalising from two cases is a hasty generalisation; a broad claim needs far more evidence.
Distractors name flaws not present: personal attack, circularity, or rejecting clicks as a measure.

items.prompt: A city says its new bike lane cut accidents because cyclist injuries fell 20% this year. Which finding would most weaken that claim?

options.label: The lane cost more than the city first planned to spend
More residents bought bicycles after the lane opened
Cyclists using the lane say they feel safer riding on it
Injuries fell about 20% on streets with no new bike lane

rubric: If injuries fell equally elsewhere, something else explains the drop, so the lane is not shown to be the cause.
Feelings of safety, cost and bike purchases do not test whether the lane caused the decline.

items.prompt: Premise 1: If it rains, the match is cancelled. Premise 2: The match was not cancelled. Which conclusion follows?

options.label: Nothing can be concluded about the rain
It did not rain
It rained, but the match was played anyway
The weather was sunny all day

rubric: Denying the consequent shows the condition did not occur (modus tollens).
Learners who say nothing follows confuse this with the invalid denial of the antecedent.

items.prompt: A researcher wants to learn whether city residents exercise regularly and surveys 500 gym members. Which change best fixes the sampling problem?

options.label: Randomly select 500 residents from the city's population register
Survey 5,000 gym members, since a larger sample removes bias
Ask the gym members more detailed questions about their routines
Survey only members who joined the gym this month

rubric: The sample must represent residents; random selection from the population does that.
A bigger or more detailed gym sample keeps the same bias.

items.prompt: Maya says, "We should shorten meetings to 30 minutes." Tom replies, "So you want us to stop discussing anything important?" Which reply best corrects Tom's distortion?

options.label: You are being dramatic, and you always exaggerate what people say in meetings
I only said 30 minutes; agendas would keep important items on the table
Everyone else on the team already agrees with me about this
Meetings were perfectly fine until you joined the team last year

rubric: The reply restates her actual position and answers the distortion, countering the straw man.
Other options attack Tom, appeal to the crowd, or blame him, which do not restore her claim.

items.prompt: A firm emails 1,000 customers. Only 40 reply, and 30 of them say they love the product. Which conclusion is best supported?

options.label: The product is disliked, because 960 customers chose not to answer
75% of all 1,000 customers love the product, so we can advertise that
30 of 40 repliers liked it, but a 4% reply rate may not represent everyone
Most customers love it, because 30 is a large number of fans

rubric: The result describes respondents only; low response may bias it, limiting generalisation.
Distractors overgeneralise, misread a raw count, or treat silence as dislike.

items.prompt: A researcher tests whether a meditation app reduces stress. Which steps would make the conclusion stronger? Select all that apply.

options.label: Recruit only people who already love meditation
Compare app users with a similar group not using the app
Assign participants to the two groups at random
Report only the participants whose stress dropped

rubric: A comparison group and random assignment help rule out other explanations for stress changes.
Recruiting enthusiasts and reporting only successes introduce selection and cherry-picking bias.

items.prompt: A shop's sales rose 15% in the month after it redesigned its logo, and the owner wants to credit the logo. Sales also rose in that same month last year. Which next step best tests the owner's claim?

options.label: Redesign the logo again and watch whether sales rise even more
Ask the staff whether they like the new logo more than the old
Check whether the new logo uses the shop's established brand colours
Compare the rise with last year's and with similar shops that kept the old logo

rubric: Comparing against seasonal patterns and similar shops without the change isolates the logo's effect.
Staff opinion, a second redesign, or brand colours do not control for seasonality or other causes.

items.prompt: A consultant argues: 'Ignore Priya's proposal to shorten meetings; she has missed three deadlines this quarter.' Which fallacy does this reasoning commit?

options.label: False dilemma: it offers two options when more actually exist
Circular reasoning: it assumes the conclusion in its premise
Ad hominem: it attacks the person rather than the proposal
Straw man: it misstates the proposal to make it easier to refute

rubric: The argument dismisses the proposal because of the proposer's record, which is ad hominem.
Straw man is tempting, but the proposal itself is never misrepresented.

items.prompt: Premises: If a report is peer reviewed, it appears in the journal index. This report does not appear in the index. Which conclusion follows validly?

options.label: The report is not peer reviewed
Nothing follows about peer review
The report is peer reviewed but was missed
The report is probably of low quality

rubric: Denying the consequent (modus tollens) validly gives 'not peer reviewed'.
Distractors confuse validity with likelihood or treat the rule as one-way and uninformative.

items.prompt: Argument: 'A new bus line opened in March, and by June downtown traffic had fallen 10%, so the bus line reduced traffic.' Which unstated assumption must hold for the conclusion to follow?

options.label: The bus line was cheaper to run than widening the roads would be
Traffic fell by the same amount in every district of the city
Most downtown commuters switched to riding the bus every single day
No other change, such as fuel prices or road works, explains the drop

rubric: A causal claim from before-and-after data assumes no other factor caused the change.
Other options add details that the inference does not require.

items.prompt: To support the claim 'weekly tutoring raises students' exam scores', which evidence is strongest?

options.label: Glowing testimonials from tutored students about feeling more confident
Scores of students randomly assigned to tutoring or to no tutoring
Higher average scores among students who chose to attend tutoring
A teacher's report that tutored students seemed more engaged in class

rubric: Random assignment with a comparison group isolates the effect of tutoring.
Self-selected groups, testimonials and impressions are confounded or not measures of scores.

items.prompt: A councillor says: 'Either we cut the library budget by half, or the city goes bankrupt.' What is the best first step in testing this argument?

options.label: Check whether the councillor has a personal stake in the library
Look for other options, such as raising revenue or trimming other budgets
Ask how many residents use the library each week
Accept it, since bankruptcy is serious enough to justify the cut

rubric: The claim is a false dilemma, so the first step is to check whether other options exist.
Other options address motive, usage or severity, not whether the two options are exhaustive.

items.prompt: Which of the following arguments commit a fallacy? Select all that apply.

options.label: 'If we allow one late submission, soon nobody will submit on time.'
'Two independent audits found the same errors, so the process needs review.'
'The study was funded by the manufacturer, so its result must be false.'
'Everyone at our office uses this app, so it must be secure.'

rubric: The first is bandwagon, the second dismisses a claim by its source (genetic fallacy), the fourth is an unsupported slippery slope.
The audit argument uses independent converging evidence and is reasonable.

items.prompt: A colleague says a new onboarding video cut customer churn, because churn fell 15% in the month after launch. You want to test this claim fairly. Which step is best?

options.label: Wait another month and check whether churn stays lower
Compare churn for customers who saw the video with similar customers who did not, over the same period
Ask the colleague how confident they are in the video's quality
Survey customers who liked the video about why they stayed

rubric: A concurrent comparison group controls for seasonal and other changes that coincide with launch.
Waiting or surveying fans does not separate the video's effect from other factors.

items.prompt: 'Most billionaires dropped out of college, so dropping out is a good route to wealth.' Which flaw best explains why this evidence is weak?

options.label: It attacks college graduates instead of addressing the argument
It counts only the dropouts who succeeded and ignores the many who did not
It treats wealth as the only measure of a good life
It relies on an authority who may be biased toward the conclusion

rubric: This is survivorship bias: the sample includes only successful cases, so the success rate of dropouts is unknown.
Other options name flaws that are not present in the argument as stated.

items.prompt: Argument: 'The city should ban cars from downtown, because this would cut downtown air pollution.' Which unstated premise is most essential to the conclusion?

options.label: Other cities that banned cars saw their air quality improve
Cars are a major pollution source downtown, and the cut justifies a ban
Most residents drive downtown daily and would oppose a ban
Air pollution is the only harm that cars cause downtown

rubric: The argument needs cars to be a real source of the pollution and the benefit to be worth a ban.
Other options are about opposition, precedent or exclusivity, which the conclusion does not depend on.

items.prompt: Three of five pilot stores raised sales after a redesign, so the argument concludes a chainwide rollout will raise sales. Which finding most weakens this inference?

options.label: Customers in the pilot stores praised the new layout in comments
The three stores were chosen because they sit in fast-growing neighbourhoods
The redesign cost more than an average store makeover
Store managers were enthusiastic about the redesign before launch

rubric: If the successful stores were unrepresentative, growth may explain the gain and the result will not generalise.
Other findings concern cost, mood or opinion, not whether the sample represents the chain.

items.prompt: Step 1: 40 gym members were surveyed and 80% supported longer hours. Step 2: The members surveyed are typical of all customers. Step 3: So most customers want longer hours. Which step needs the most support?

options.label: Step 2: nothing shows the surveyed members represent all customers
Step 1: a survey cannot measure support for a policy at all
Step 3: a majority can never justify a conclusion about customers
No step: the argument is valid because the percentage is high

rubric: The inference to all customers depends on representativeness, which is assumed, not shown.
Surveys can measure support, and a high percentage does not fix a sampling gap.

items.prompt: Sam says, 'Let's review the budget before we approve new hires.' Lee replies, 'So you want to freeze all hiring for good?' Which description of Lee's reply is most accurate?

options.label: False dilemma: it says the only choices are review or hiring
Straw man: it recasts a call for review as an extreme freeze
Ad hominem: it attacks Sam's character rather than the proposal
Equivocation: it shifts the meaning of 'review' midway through

rubric: Lee replaces Sam's moderate position with an exaggerated one that is easier to attack.
Lee does not attack Sam personally, offer exactly two options or change a word's meaning.

items.prompt: Claim: 'Employees who use standing desks report higher productivity, so standing desks raise productivity.' Which findings would weaken the causal inference? Select all that apply.

options.label: The company in the study has about 300 employees
Standing desk makers advertise widely to large companies
Productivity was self-reported by employees who paid for the desks themselves
Employees who volunteered for standing desks were already the top performers

rubric: Prior high performance (selection) and biased self-reports from people who invested in the desks both offer alternative explanations.
Advertising reach and company size do not bear on whether desks caused the difference.

items.prompt: A town installed speed cameras at its ten worst accident sites, chosen because they had unusually high crash counts last year. Crashes at those sites fell 30% the next year, and an analyst says the cameras caused the drop. Which is the most important weakness in this analysis?

options.label: The analyst may profit from camera sales and be biased in the result
Ten sites is too many for a town of that size to analyse properly
Extreme counts tend to fall back toward normal, so some drop would occur without cameras
Cameras only catch speeding and cannot affect other causes of crashes

rubric: Sites picked for unusually high counts tend to regress toward the mean, which can mimic a treatment effect.
Other options raise motive, scope or scale, none of which explains the selection effect.

items.prompt: Hospital A has a higher overall survival rate than Hospital B. Yet when patients are split into mild, moderate and severe cases, B has the higher survival rate in every group. What is the best diagnosis of this pattern?

options.label: Hospital A has treated more patients, so its overall rate is more reliable than the subgroup rates.
The subgroup figures must contain errors, because subgroup results cannot contradict the overall result.
The hospitals differ in how many severe cases they treat, so the aggregate figure is distorted by case mix.
Averaging across groups always favours the larger hospital, so the aggregate figure is the fairest one.

rubric: Unequal group sizes (confounding by case mix) can reverse an aggregate trend, as in Simpson's paradox.
Distractors assume aggregates and subgroups must agree, or that sample size resolves the conflict.

items.prompt: A city says: 'Crime fell 12% in the year after our new patrol policy, so the policy works.' Records show crime had already fallen about 10% every year for five years. Which weakness is most damaging to the claim?

options.label: The 12% fall barely exceeds the existing trend, so most of the drop would likely have happened without the policy.
The claim covers only one year, so a longer follow-up is needed before any conclusion about the policy is drawn.
The claim uses police-recorded crime, so the figures may be affected by changes in how often residents report incidents.
The claim relies on a single city, so the result cannot be generalised to other cities with different populations.

rubric: The pre-existing trend offers a baseline that explains nearly all of the change, which undermines attribution.
Other options name real limits but do not address the specific trend evidence given.

items.prompt: A product team argues: 'Users who enable notifications retain 40% better, so we should switch notifications on for everyone.' Which hidden assumption does the argument most depend on?

options.label: Enabling notifications causes better retention, rather than already-engaged users being the ones who opt in.
Users who disabled notifications did so by mistake, so they will welcome being switched back on later.
Retention is the right metric for success, so other measures such as satisfaction need not be considered.
Notifications are cheap to send, so switching them on for everyone adds no meaningful cost to the product.

rubric: The argument moves from a correlation to an intervention, which requires a causal link rather than self-selection.
Other options are side assumptions, not the one the inference depends on.

items.prompt: A reviewer writes: 'This nutrition study was funded by a soda company, so its finding that sugar is harmless is false.' What is the flaw in this reasoning?

options.label: It confuses the study's sample size with its funding source, and so draws a conclusion unrelated to the evidence.
It treats the study's funding as proof of falsity, rather than a reason to examine its methods and data.
It ignores that industry funding makes a study more rigorous, because companies stake their reputation on results.
It assumes that company-funded studies are always biased, which is true often enough that the inference is reasonable.

rubric: Attacking the source (genetic fallacy) is not evidence about the claim; funding justifies scrutiny only.
Distractors either defend the inference or invent a different confusion.

items.prompt: A business book studies 50 hugely successful firms and finds all took big risks and had charismatic founders. It concludes that bold risk-taking and charisma produce success. What is the main flaw in the method?

options.label: The book mixes correlation with causation, but the traits it names are plausible causes, so the conclusion stands.
Charisma is subjective and hard to measure, so the book cannot say whether the founders really shared this trait.
Fifty firms is too few to establish a pattern, so a larger sample would be enough to make the conclusion safe.
The book selects on the outcome, so it never checks how many failed firms were equally bold and charismatic.

rubric: Sampling only successes (survivorship bias) cannot show whether the traits distinguish winners from losers.
Distractors suggest more data or measurement fixes would be enough, or excuse the inference.

items.prompt: A school reports that students who joined a voluntary tutoring programme after a poor test improved by 15 points on the next test, and claims the programme caused it. There was no comparison group. Which factors could explain the gain without the programme working? Select all that apply.

options.label: The tutors were described by students as friendly and approachable.
Students chosen after an unusually low score tend to score closer to their average next time.
Students usually improve during the term through ordinary teaching and practice.
The programme enrolled 200 students, which is a fairly large group.
Students who volunteer tend to be more motivated than those who do not.

rubric: Self-selection, regression to the mean and maturation are alternative explanations when there is no control group.
Group size and tutor friendliness do not offer a rival explanation for the gain.

items.prompt: A screening test for a disease is 95% accurate: it detects 95% of sick people and wrongly flags 5% of healthy ones. The disease affects 1 in 1,000 people. A friend tests positive and says, 'So there is a 95% chance I have it.' What is wrong with this reasoning?

options.label: It assumes the test is random, whereas a 95% accurate test cannot be wrong more than once in twenty uses on one person.
It ignores that a second test is needed, so the chance is exactly 50% until a repeat test gives the same result.
It confuses sensitivity with specificity, but the two figures are equal here, so the 95% chance is roughly right.
It ignores how rare the disease is, so most positives come from the large healthy group and the real chance is far below 95%.

rubric: Base-rate neglect: with 1 in 1,000 prevalence, about 50 false positives arise per true positive, so the chance is under 2%.
Distractors keep the 95% idea or invent a fixed 50% figure.

items.prompt: A government claims a new policy cut youth unemployment in the regions that adopted it. You must pick the added evidence that would best support a causal reading. Which should you choose?

options.label: A survey of local employers in adopting regions showing broad approval of the policy and its design.
Data from similar non-adopting regions over the same period, with matching unemployment trends before the policy.
A longer run of data from adopting regions only, showing unemployment staying low for several more years.
Interviews with several young people in adopting regions who say the policy helped them find work.

rubric: A comparison group with parallel pre-trends controls for background change and isolates the policy effect.
Testimonials, longer one-group data and approval ratings cannot rule out other causes.

items.prompt: You must judge evidence for a drug's effect, prioritising protection against bias and chance. Which source deserves the most weight?

options.label: An observational cohort of 50,000 users showing better outcomes, with users choosing the drug themselves.
A review of 12 small unregistered trials, mostly positive, in which small studies show larger effects than large ones.
An editorial by a respected specialist who has treated hundreds of patients and recommends the drug strongly.
A preregistered randomised trial of 300 patients with a modest, clearly reported effect and low dropout.

rubric: Randomisation and preregistration best guard against confounding and selective reporting.
Distractors rely on size, expertise or pooling that cannot fix bias.

items.prompt: In a meeting, a colleague dismisses a report by saying, 'Citing a physician on a medical question is an appeal to authority, which is a fallacy.' Which assessment of that objection is best?

options.label: It is right, because any reliance on an expert in place of direct evidence is a fallacy in formal logic.
It is right only if the physician is famous, since fame is what turns an expert's view into a fallacy.
It is wrong, because experts are always correct within their field, so citing one settles the question.
It is wrong in general, since relevant expert consensus is legitimate evidence, though not conclusive and open to challenge.

rubric: Appeal to authority is fallacious when the authority is irrelevant, unrepresentative or treated as infallible.
Distractors either ban all expert evidence or treat experts as infallible.

items.prompt: A pharmacy ad says a supplement 'cuts your risk of a certain illness by 50%'. The illness affects 2 in 10,000 people without it and 1 in 10,000 with it. The supplement costs 30 dollars a month. Which judgement is best supported?

options.label: The claim is accurate and the benefit is large, so buying it is justified for anyone worried about the illness.
The claim should be ignored, because any advertisement for a supplement is by nature unreliable as evidence.
The relative figure exaggerates a tiny absolute gain, so the cost per event prevented should drive the decision.
The claim is misleading because the figures are invalid, since a 50% cut would require a much larger starting risk.

rubric: A 50% relative cut is only 0.01 percentage points absolute, so about 10,000 people must be treated to prevent one case.
Distractors accept the framing, wrongly call the numbers invalid, or reject the claim by its source.

items.prompt: An analyst has two explanations for a sales dip: (1) a competitor's price cut, which predicts losses concentrated in price-sensitive segments, and (2) 'general market mood', which predicts nothing specific. Judging by testability and explanatory power, which is better?

options.label: Explanation 2, because it fits any pattern of results and so can never be contradicted by the data.
Explanation 2, because it is simpler and uses fewer details, and simpler explanations are always preferred.
Explanation 1, because it makes a specific prediction that existing segment data could disconfirm.
Explanation 1, because the competitor is a named cause and named causes are more likely to be true.

rubric: Good explanations take a risk: they forbid outcomes and can be checked against data.
An explanation that fits everything explains nothing; simplicity cannot rescue it.

items.prompt: You are judging whether an argument gives good reason to accept its conclusion. Which criteria properly bear on its strength? Select all that apply.

options.label: The argument has been repeated by many people across several media.
The premises are acceptable, meaning supported by good evidence or common ground.
The argument deals fairly with the strongest counterevidence and objections.
The conclusion matches what most listeners already believe and would like to hear.
The premises are relevant to the conclusion and give it real support.

rubric: Acceptable premises, relevance and a response to counterevidence are standard tests of argument quality.
Popularity and agreeableness of a conclusion are not evidence for it.

items.prompt: A school board must decide whether later start times raise grades. Study 1 randomly assigned 6 schools to start later and compared grades after one semester. Study 2 surveyed 40 schools and found later starts correlated with better self-reported attendance. Which approach to weighing the studies is best?

options.label: Average the two results, because combining different designs cancels their individual errors and gives balance.
Give Study 1 most weight on causation for grades, noting its short span and few schools, and use Study 2 for hypotheses.
Reject both studies, because neither is perfect, and delay any decision until a flawless study is available.
Trust Study 2 most, because 40 schools is a much larger sample and a larger sample always yields firmer conclusions.

rubric: Randomisation supports causal claims on grades, while Study 2 is correlational and measures another outcome.
Distractors favour sample size, blur designs by averaging, or demand perfection.

items.prompt: A reviewer rejects a drug trial solely because the manufacturer paid for it. Judged by the criteria of fairness to the evidence and protection against bias, which assessment is best?

options.label: Caution is justified only when the trial found a benefit, since null results from a funded trial cannot reflect any sponsor bias.
Funding justifies closer scrutiny of design and reporting, but dismissing results by their source alone is a genetic fallacy.
Funding is irrelevant to evidence quality, so the reviewer should ignore it and judge only the headline result the trial reports.
Industry funding makes the conclusions false by default, so the reviewer is right to discard the trial without reading its methods.

rubric: Source is a reason to check methods, not a refutation; rejecting by origin is the genetic fallacy.
Distractors swing to ignoring funding entirely or treating it as automatic falsity.

items.prompt: A screening test is 99% sensitive and 99% specific for a condition affecting 1 in 1,000 people. A columnist argues a positive result means a 99% chance of having the condition. Which critique is strongest?

options.label: It confuses sensitivity with specificity, so the true figure is simply the average of the two, which is still very close to 99%.
It treats one test as decisive, whereas a 99% figure is only valid once the same person has tested positive twice.
It ignores the base rate: false positives from the healthy majority outnumber true positives by roughly ten to one.
It assumes the test performs the same at every age, so the figure holds only after adjusting for who was screened.

rubric: With a 0.1% prevalence, about 99 true positives arise against about 999 false positives per 100,000 people, so a positive result means roughly a 9% chance.
Distractors misread the metrics or invoke vague adjustments instead of the base-rate neglect.

items.prompt: Overall, Hospital A has a higher death rate than Hospital B, yet A has a lower rate within both mild and severe cases because it receives far more severe cases. To judge which is safer for a given patient, which reasoning is best?

options.label: Compare within severity groups, since severity drives both admission to A and survival, making stratified rates the fairer comparison.
Trust the overall rate, since it uses every patient and larger samples are always more reliable than any subgroup figures.
Treat the reversal as proof that one dataset was miscalculated or tampered with, so neither comparison can be used at all.
Average the two subgroup rates for each hospital without weighting, since the aggregate is distorted by differences in case counts.

rubric: Severity is a confounder tied to admission, so comparing like with like is more informative than the pooled rate.
Distractors defend the aggregate, suspect fraud, or use an unweighted average.

items.prompt: After a large, well-powered trial with careful follow-up found no excess liver injury, a researcher is challenged with the slogan 'absence of evidence is not evidence of absence.' Judged by sound inference, what is the best assessment?

options.label: The slogan applies here until an independent group replicates the trial, and only then is the harm proven absent for good.
The slogan is a fallacy in every case, because a lack of findings always establishes that no effect at all exists.
The slogan fails here: a search likely to detect harm that finds none is evidence against harm, though not proof.
The slogan holds universally, so no study result however large or careful can ever count as evidence that a harm is absent.

rubric: Absence of evidence counts when the search was sensitive enough to find the effect; it supports, but does not prove, absence.
Distractors treat the slogan as always true or always false.

items.prompt: A commentator argues: 'The lack of any proof of the cover-up shows how well organised it is.' Judged by whether evidence can bear on a claim, what is the most damaging critique?

options.label: It is a slippery slope, since it assumes one small concealment will inevitably grow into larger and more organised ones.
Any outcome, including no evidence, is read as support, so no observation could count against the claim and data cannot favour it.
It is an appeal to ignorance, which means that every claim lacking proof must be treated as false until someone proves it.
It is circular only because the commentator never names who is responsible, so naming a group would make it sound.

rubric: The claim is unfalsifiable: it predicts the same observation whether true or false, so evidence cannot discriminate.
Distractors mislabel it with other fallacies or suggest a trivial fix.

items.prompt: A cohort study finds coffee drinkers have lower rates of a disease. Which features would most strengthen a judgement that coffee causally reduces risk? Select all that apply.

options.label: Risk falls steadily as daily intake rises across several intake levels
The sample was very large, so the association is highly significant
A natural experiment, such as a price shock, shows the same effect
Drinkers reported feeling healthier than non-drinkers in the study
Coffee intake was recorded before any participant developed the disease

rubric: Dose-response, temporal order and quasi-experimental replication address causal direction and confounding.
Sample size and self-reported wellbeing do not address confounding or direction.

items.prompt: An analyst reviews two arguments for adopting a résumé-screening model. Argument 1: it matches past hiring decisions 95% of the time. Argument 2: in a pilot, its picks had 10% better 12-month performance reviews than randomly chosen, equally qualified applicants. The criterion is evidence that it selects good employees rather than copying past choices. Which judgement is best?

options.label: The two are equally strong, since each relies on a single metric and neither can show the model beats human judgement.
Argument 2 is weaker because a pilot is smaller than the historical data, and sample size alone decides argument quality here.
Argument 2 is stronger because it measures an outcome, though review bias and a short horizon limit it; Argument 1 shows only imitation.
Argument 1 is stronger because a 95% match shows the model has captured what the firm already knows to be good hiring practice.

rubric: Matching past decisions measures imitation, including past bias; a comparison on later performance speaks to selection quality.
Distractors equate agreement with validity or judge by sample size alone.

items.prompt: You must test whether a meditation app reduces anxiety. Constraints: rule out placebo effects and self-selection of motivated users, and prevent the outcome measure from being chosen after seeing results. Which design meets all three?

options.label: Randomly assign volunteers to the app or a similar-looking non-meditation app, and pre-register the measure and analysis plan.
Compare existing app users with non-users on anxiety after three months, adjusting for age, income and prior therapy use.
Give all volunteers the app, measure anxiety before and after, and report whichever scale shows the largest improvement.
Randomly assign volunteers to the app or a waiting list, and pick the best-performing outcome measure after data collection ends.

rubric: Random assignment handles self-selection, an active control handles placebo, and pre-registration fixes the outcome.
Other options miss at least one constraint.

items.prompt: Claim: 'Many billionaire founders dropped out of college, so dropping out boosts your chance of success.' Which revision of the argument would support a well-founded conclusion?

options.label: Survey the dropouts about why they think they succeeded, and treat their shared explanation as the causal evidence.
Add many more examples of successful dropouts until the list is long enough that coincidence becomes statistically unlikely.
Restrict the claim to billionaires and argue that, because dropouts are common among them, dropping out is necessary.
Compare the share reaching success among dropouts with that among graduates who start companies, matching on starting circumstances.

rubric: The original selects on the outcome; a valid test compares success rates across both groups, including failures.
Distractors keep sampling on success or rely on self-report.

items.prompt: To refute the claim 'any argument with a true premise and a true conclusion is valid', which counterexample works?

options.label: Premise: Paris is in France. Conclusion: Grass is green. Both are true, yet the conclusion does not follow from the premise.
Premise: The moon is made of cheese. Conclusion: Cheese exists. The conclusion is true although the premise is false.
Premise: All dogs are mammals. Conclusion: Some mammals are dogs. Both true, and the conclusion follows from the premise.
Premise: All birds fly. Conclusion: Penguins fly. The reasoning is valid but both statements are in fact false.

rubric: A counterexample needs a true premise, a true conclusion and a failure of entailment.
Distractors are valid, have a false premise, or are valid with false statements.

items.prompt: A team's procedure for testing its theory says: 'We will keep the theory if the results are consistent with it.' What key element is missing from this design?

options.label: A larger budget, so that more confirming data can be gathered before any final decision about the theory is made.
A statement made beforehand of which results would count against the theory, so consistency cannot be claimed for any outcome.
A rule that the most senior member decides whether the results are consistent, to keep interpretation uniform across the team.
A second theory from the same team that predicts identical results, so that any confirmation is checked twice over.

rubric: Without prespecified disconfirming outcomes, 'consistent' can be stretched to fit anything.
Distractors add more confirmation, redundancy or authority, none of which address falsifiability.

items.prompt: A three-city observational study finds neighbourhoods with more green space have lower depression rates, even after adjusting for income. Which conclusion is best supported and most useful to decision makers?

options.label: The association is probably an artefact, because adjusting for income always removes the real effect of any neighbourhood feature.
Adjustment for income shows green space lowers depression, so the causal effect is established and cities should expand parks now.
No conclusion is allowed, since observational studies from only three cities give no evidence about the causes of depression.
Green space is associated with lower depression after income adjustment; residual confounding remains, so test causation with a trial.

rubric: A calibrated claim states the association, names the limit and proposes a stronger test.
Distractors overclaim causation, dismiss the finding, or reject all observational evidence.

items.prompt: You are designing a review process for a persuasive proposal that reduces confirmation bias. Which elements belong in it? Select all that apply.

options.label: Circulate only supporting evidence to keep discussion focused
Seek data from sources likely to disagree with the proposal
Write down beforehand what evidence would make the team abandon it
Assign a reviewer to build the strongest case against the proposal
Ask the author to rate their confidence before the meeting

rubric: Devil's advocacy, prespecified disconfirmation and disagreeing sources counter confirmation bias.
Confidence ratings and supporting-only evidence do not, and the latter worsens it.

items.prompt: A health agency must write a memo on whether a new school-lunch policy cut absenteeism. Absenteeism fell 8% after rollout, but flu was mild that year, and three comparable districts without the policy have data. The memo must separate the policy effect from other causes and state uncertainty. Which plan best meets this?

options.label: Compare the change in absenteeism in policy districts with the change in comparison districts over the same period, with a confidence range.
Survey parents on whether they believe the lunches helped, and report the share who agree as the size of the effect.
Report the 8% fall as the policy effect, noting in a footnote that the flu season was milder than usual that year.
Compare policy districts' absenteeism with the national average over earlier decades, and report that gap as the effect.

rubric: A difference-in-differences comparison nets out shared shocks like mild flu and allows uncertainty to be stated.
Distractors ignore confounders, use opinion, or use a non-contemporaneous baseline.
